needs.definition: A day on which a member of the household cannot reach the files, accounts and working computer they rely on for work, records and money: documents, photos, tax, insurance and medical records, passwords and the tools of their trade. Only what is out of reach counts; news and contact are the information need, and the ability to pay is the payments need.

baselineCoverageDays.basis: Nothing ordinary in a home replaces files that are out of reach. What a phone or a synced folder still holds is counted in the share of each window that opens the need (notes), not as days of cover.

hardshipUsdPerPersonDay.basis: 27% of US paid workdays are worked from home (WFH Research via FRED, October 2026: 27.06%; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WFHCOVIDMATQUESTION). If a fifth of those rely on the household's own computer or files, and a day without them costs about $100 after the work made up later, that is about $5 per working adult-day; with records, bills, schoolwork and personal projects ($1-2) and averaged over members, about $4 at first. It rises as bills, claims and deadlines are missed. Lo: almost everything is on the phone or the employer's machine. Hi: a self-employed member whose livelihood is on the computer.

mortalityMicromortsPerPersonDay.basis: None: being without one's files is not dangerous. Records matter for health only through medication and emergency care, which are other needs.

multipliers.basis: Children lose only schoolwork and games, and schools supply their own devices and accounts.

openedBy.hazards: every hazard with a comms window (commsOutage, cyberOutage, gridLong, greatPowerWar, storms)

share.basis: Share of a household's essential files and tools that live only online (web documents, cloud-only photo libraries, online records, web apps). 78% of consumers use free cloud storage and 45% an external drive (Western Digital and Researchscape, 6,118 respondents, February 2025: https://www.techedt.com/most-consumers-now-back-up-their-data-but-cloud-storage-limits-push-shift-to-hybrid-solutions); synced folders keep local copies, streamed ones do not.

openedBy.hazards: aiFraud: account takeover, a fraud lock or lost second factor, and ransomware on household devices

pOccur.basis: Share of aiFraud events (6% a year per US household, ai-economy.json) in which an email, cloud or device account holding the household's files is taken or locked, rather than money alone lost. Security.org (1,062 US adults, December 2023): 29% of adults have had an account taken over, 'about one in five victims' within the last year (about 6% of adults a year), and 23% of victims lost an email or messaging account: about 1.3% of adults, or 2.6% of two-adult households, a year (https://www.security.org/digital-safety/account-takeover-annual-report/).

openedBy.basis: Google: 'Account recovery requests can be delayed for a few hours or a number of days, depending on a variety of risk factors' (https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/9412469); accounts without a working second factor take longer, and some are never recovered.

openedBy.hazards: wildfire, hurricane, flood, earthquake and any hazard that displaces

share.basis: Chance that the household's computer is left behind or destroyed when it must leave. The unmet days are those until a replacement is bought and files restored from the cloud: the displacement days, but at most about a week.

needs.notes: Three things open the need. (1) A comms window makes cloud-only files and web-only tools unreachable, for the share above. (2) Ransomware, a wiped device or a locked account takes the files or the computer itself away; in the model this belongs in aiFraud, which has no window now, or in an everyday device-loss hazard (open questions). (3) The computer is destroyed in a fire, flood or earthquake, or left behind when the household is displaced; houseFire has no windows, so only the displacement route applies there. The existing data-backup item (money-docs.json) is a cloud and automatic backup valued on the financial loss of records and photos after a fire; it does not keep the household working while the network, the account or the computer is unavailable, and a synced cloud copy can be overwritten by encrypted files.

items.name: Offline backup and spare computer
items.spec: A 2 TB portable drive, encrypted (BitLocker, FileVault or the drive's own password), holding the household's essential files and refreshed monthly, then unplugged and kept in the go-bag or away from home; plus a spare laptop, either an old one kept charged and updated or a cheap new one, holding the same essentials, a password-manager emergency kit, and offline copies of the tools needed to work (an office suite, a PDF reader, installers, any cloud-only documents exported to files). Both are tested twice a year by opening a few files on the spare machine with the network off.
items.unit: backup drive and spare laptop for the household

usdPerUnit.basis: Read on retailer pages on 20 November 2026, when storage prices were two to three times their 2024-25 level. Drive: Seagate Expansion 2 TB $95.99 (Staples, out of stock), WD Elements 2 TB $169.99 on sale (Target), Seagate One Touch 2 TB with password $163.99 (Zones); software encryption (FileVault, BitLocker, VeraCrypt) is free. Spare laptop: refurbished Lenovo ThinkPad T490 $209.99 or T14 Gen 1 $304.99, new HP 14 (N150, 4 GB) $299.99, Acer Aspire Go 15 $459.99 (all Target). Lo: drive only, the old laptop serving as the spare. Mid: a $170 drive and a refurbished business laptop or a cheap new one, about $230 more. Hi: a 2 TB portable SSD ($458-575, SanDisk Extreme or Samsung T7 Shield) and a $300 laptop.

price.product: WD Elements 2 TB portable drive and a refurbished Lenovo ThinkPad T490

lifeYears.basis: A portable drive and a cheap laptop each last about five years; an old laptop kept as the spare is already part-way through its life, and its operating system may stop receiving updates.

setupHours.basis: Choosing what is essential, exporting cloud-only documents, encrypting the drive, setting up the spare laptop and writing down the passwords needed to open both.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: About five minutes a month to refresh the drive and twenty minutes a quarter to update and charge the spare laptop, plus two short restore tests.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: None beyond electricity; hi allows for a paid backup utility.

everydayShare.basis: An offline copy and a second computer protect against drive failure, theft, breakage and ransomware, which happen far more often than any regional event: about 5% of devices a year fail or are lost (money-docs.json, data-backup, recalled), and about 6% of adults a year have an account taken over (Security.org). Lower than data-backup's 0.95 because the spare laptop and the monthly unplugging are bought for resilience, not convenience.

reliability.basis: Failures: a copy months out of date, a forgotten encryption password, a spare laptop with a flat battery or an expired operating system, essentials that were never copied.

fractionRemoved.basis: With the network down, a household that would otherwise improvise with its phone and whatever synced folders hold can open its cloud-only documents, records and photos and do offline work (writing, spreadsheets, accounts). Work that needs the network is not restored.

adherence.basis: The household remembers the copy and the outage lasts long enough to fetch it.

effects.notes: Acts only on the share of comms days that opens dataAccess (needs, openedBy). In cyberOutage the spare laptop also doubles the hours of computing on battery; not claimed.

fractionRemoved.basis: After ransomware, a wiped device or a locked account, an unplugged copy and a second computer restore the files and a working machine at once; what remains is the locked account itself (its email, its online services).

adherence.basis: A household locked out has every reason to use it.

effects.notes: Requires the dataAccess window in aiFraud proposed under needs.openedBy.

fractionRemoved.basis: Only if the drive is in the go-bag or away from home; the spare laptop is usually left behind or lost with the main one. With the drive, any borrowed or new computer has the files the same day instead of after a cloud restore.

adherence.basis: The drive was where the plan said when the household left.

effects.description: Protects the household's records and photos against loss, not just unavailability, where ransomware or a takeover destroys both the computer's copy and the synced cloud copy: CISA advises offline, encrypted backups because 'if local files are encrypted by an attacker, these files will be synced to the cloud, possibly overwriting unaffected data'. The data-backup item values that loss after a fire; here it would be a small addition to aiFraud's financialLoss, not claimed.

evidence.claim: Sentinel (19 November 2026), after forecasting 33% for a week-long OECD outage by end-2028: 'keep an offline backup of your important data and perhaps a backup computer in case your main one gets hacked.'

CISA, FBI, NSA and MS-ISAC, #StopRansomware Guide: 'Maintain offline, encrypted backups of critical data, and regularly test the availability and integrity of backups'; 'Automated cloud backups may not be sufficient because if local files are encrypted by an attacker, these files will be synced to the cloud, possibly overwriting unaffected data.'
Western Digital and Researchscape (6,118 consumers, February 2025): 87% back up, 78% use free cloud storage, 45% use external hard drives.
Google: 'Account recovery requests can be delayed for a few hours or a number of days, depending on a variety of risk factors.'

items.notes: Distinct from data-backup (money-docs.json): that is a cloud service and an always-connected drive, valued on records and photos lost in a fire; it cannot be read without the network and can be overwritten by ransomware. This entry is a disconnected copy and a second machine, valued on days of access to files and a working computer. A household with an old laptop pays only for the drive.

items.name: Offline reference library
items.spec: Kiwix (free) on a laptop with the full English Wikipedia (119 GB) and on each phone with the 'mini' edition (13 GB) or the edition without pictures (49 GB); Wikipedia's medicine collection (WikiMed, 1.7 GB); iFixit repair guides (3.3 GB), Wikivoyage (1 GB) and Stack Exchange's DIY, cooking and gardening sites (about 3 GB); and a handful of practical books in PDF. Refreshed once a year. Plus two paper books for when the battery is flat: the SAS Survival Handbook and a home-repair manual (Black & Decker's Book of Home How-To). The paper first-aid manual and lay medical handbook are a separate entry (reference-books).

usdPerUnit.basis: Kiwix and its collections are free on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS (https://get.kiwix.org/en/solutions/applications/kiwix-reader/). Paperbacks at Barnes & Noble, 20 November 2026: SAS Survival Handbook $25.99, Black & Decker The Book of Home How-To $40.00, The Encyclopedia of Country Living $29.95. Lo: one book, downloads on storage the household has. Mid: two books. Hi: three books and a 256 GB microSD card for a phone too full for Wikipedia (SanDisk Ultra $62.99 at Target).

price.product: SAS Survival Handbook and Black & Decker The Book of Home How-To (paperbacks); Kiwix downloads

lifeYears.basis: The downloads are refreshed yearly at no cost; the card and the paper books last five to twenty years.

setupHours.basis: Installing Kiwix, choosing and downloading collections (large downloads run unattended), buying the books and finding where the medical pages are.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly refresh of the downloads.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Kiwix and its collections are free.

everydayShare.basis: Looking things up on flights, abroad without data or in places without signal, and reading the books.

reliability.basis: The device must be charged and the files present; the household must remember it has them and find the right page under stress. The paper books cover a flat battery.

fractionRemoved.basis: The information need's $15 day (comms.json) is news and instructions ($11.25), contact ($10.50) and ordinary use ($3.25), of which looking things up is a part. An encyclopedia and how-to library recovers perhaps a sixth of ordinary use ($0.55) plus a little practical guidance in long outages: about 4% of the day, beside offline entertainment's 5% and offline maps' 3%. Nothing for news or contact.

adherence.basis: Used when a question comes up and the network is down.

effects.notes: On hardship only: it does not let anyone call for help.

fractionRemoved.basis: As reference-books (0.01): only where care is out of reach for weeks. WikiMed is fuller and searchable but needs a charged screen and is slower to use in an emergency than a paper manual. No study measures the effect of owning either.

effects.notes: Near-perfect substitute for reference-books on this channel: a household that owns one gains almost nothing on trauma from the other, and the model's multiplicative combination overstates the pair.

effects.description: In long outages, practical knowledge (treating water, cooking without power, repairing things, identifying illness) improves the improvisation that other needs' curves already assume. The model has no way to credit it; not claimed.

evidence.claim: Sentinel (19 November 2026): 'Perhaps keep offline copies of wikipedia or other' references, 'or even useful physical books'.
Kiwix's English Wikipedia files: with pictures 119 GB (August 2026), without pictures 49 GB (June 2026), 'mini' 13 GB (September 2026); medicine collection 1.7 GB with pictures (October 2026).
Kiwix Reader is 'completely free' on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS; 'only our Hotspot packages and custom services come at a price'.
No study measures any effect of owning an offline encyclopedia or reference books in a disaster; the step 2 longlist cites recommendations only (The Prepared, CDC).

items.notes: Distinct from reference-books (plans-skills-security.json), a paper first-aid manual and lay medical handbook kept with the first-aid kit: this entry is mostly digital, general rather than medical, and needs a charged device; its paper books are practical, not medical.

excluded.what: Network-attached storage or a second always-connected drive
excluded.reason: Reachable by ransomware on the same network and useless without power; the existing data-backup item already covers an automatic local copy.
Durable but slow to write and to read, and most new laptops have no drive; a refreshed portable drive does the same job for a household.

excluded.what: A shielded (Faraday) bag for the spare laptop
excluded.reason: Matters only for EMP in nuclearNear and gridLong; see faraday-bag in comms.json.

excluded.what: Kiwix Hotspot or other preloaded offline servers
excluded.reason: Serve many users at once (schools, clinics); a household gets the same content free on devices it owns.
Restores the network rather than offline access; an information and comms item, outside this assignment.

blockedSources: bhphotovideo.com, newegg.com, microcenter.com, backmarket.com, adorama.com, dellrefurbished.com, lenovo.com, bookshop.org (HTTP 403); amazon.com (503); walmart.com (bot check); bestbuy.com product pages (time out): would have given more laptop, drive and book prices. Best Buy snippets show a Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i at $249.99 and an Acer Chromebook 311 at $159, unverified.

westerndigital.com, sandisk.com and seagate.com: no price shown or product no longer stocked. Search snippets showing 2 TB drives at $86-97 and 512 GB cards at $27-53 look stale against the pages read.
https://guidebooks.google.com/online-security/account-recovery/learn-about-account-recovery : empty page; a snippet says recovery delays run 'from 6 hours to 30 days', unverified.
openQuestions: dataAccess needs a gap in data/config.mjs. Proposed: the comms window at a share of 0.4 (0.2-0.7); a new dataAccess window in aiFraud (pOccur 0.3, days 3, 14, 60) for account lockout and ransomware; and the displacement window at a share of 0.4, capped at about seven days per event.

Device loss in everyday life (drive failure, theft, breakage, home ransomware; about 5% of households a year, recalled) is not a hazard in the model. If it is added with a dataAccess window (days about 3, 10, 30), the everydayShare of offline-backup-computer should fall from 0.6 to about 0.2 so that the same value is not counted twice.

research/impartial/impartial.json gives workLoss.dataAccess 0.55 (0.25-0.85) of a day, for a knowledge worker whose work needs their own documents and logins. The hardship curve here ($4 a person-day at first) averages over members, of whom perhaps 5-20% of workers depend on household files or machines for work: 27% of paid days at home x about a fifth on the household's own machine. The two should agree: either scale the impartial figure by that share (to about 0.03-0.1), or raise this curve for a member who works on a personal computer (on the order of $50-150 a day).
offline-reference and reference-books substitute for each other on trauma; the engine combines reduce effects multiplicatively, which overstates owning both.
